text: Two women come back to the Faroe Islands after seven years away, and their clothes alone are enough to start a quarrel. Katrin Ottarsdóttir shoots in Faroese, eighty-five minutes of comedy that keeps cooling into something harder: Rannvá and Barba are a spectacle to the people who raised them, and spectacle turns quickly into offence. They set out across the islands with a local man, Rúni, which makes this a road movie on ground where the roads run out. The constraint does the work. Nothing can be outdriven here, so whatever the three of them brought along stays in the car with them, and what a visitor would call scenery is for these three a list of addresses. The comedy of two women in the wrong coats becomes an account of what a homecoming costs the people who stayed.

Midnight on an unlit highway, two people who need a ride, and a car that slows down. Sanal Kumar Sasidharan sets Durga and Kabeer's flight from their village against a temple festival running the same night, where devotees give their bodies over to the goddess whose name the woman carries. The cut between those two things is the method: worship in one frame, a stranger's headlights in the next, eighty-five minutes of Malayalam that lets neither settle. What is at stake is small and enormous, a railway station reached or not reached. Every offer of help arrives as a courtesy and lands as a transaction, and the film is patient enough to let each ride run past the point where its passengers would like it to end. It took a Tiger Award.

Lynn has no plan, and the film declines to treat that as a problem in need of solving. She is twenty-two, works in a cafe, lives with her brother, and is attached to David, a swimmer whose training organises every hour he has. Maria Speth gives all this a hundred and eighteen minutes, which is a long stretch of screen time to hand to a life without a schedule, and the length is the argument: drift watched closely enough stops looking like nothing. Then Koji arrives, an exchange student who shares almost no language with her, and the centre of the film becomes two people sitting in a silence that is neither awkward nor empty. Speth trusts that quiet more than she trusts dialogue. Little is declared here; nearly everything is observed.

Chinese New Year is the week that requires everybody to be somebody's child. Muzi is twenty-two and back in Hangzhou, where that role waits for her along with two others, half-sister and girlfriend, each held out by someone who knew her before she left. Zheng Lu Xinyuan builds the film from that friction rather than from plot: a hundred and two minutes of a young woman moving through streets she can navigate without thinking and no longer recognises. The city is not standing in for anything larger than itself. It is a schedule of obligations with an address for each. What holds the film together is Muzi's attention, which keeps sliding off the people talking to her and onto rooms, weather, water, as though the family occasion were happening slightly behind her.

Real archive footage of a named prime minister, cut into a private life he never had. Morten Hartz Kaplers assembles AFR from documentary material, hired actors and computer effects, then presents the result as a broadcast: the Danish prime minister Anders Fogh Rasmussen, a secret lover called Emil, a national story told in the grammar of the evening news. The nerve of it is the method rather than the gossip. Eighty-three minutes in which genuine speeches and genuine crowds are made to carry an invention, so that the footage a viewer trusts by reflex is the part doing the lying. Denmark produced it in 2007 with the name intact and no invented republic to hide behind. A thriller by genre; a forgery by construction.

Jamil is standing in the middle of a quarrel older than he is, and it has followed his family to Scandinavia. Omar Shargawi gives it ninety minutes and a crime film's momentum, then spends most of that time arguing against exactly the momentum he has built. Religious hatred is the inheritance here; the pressure comes from whether a man can refuse an inheritance without being destroyed for refusing it. That a Danish production carries the story is not incidental. Distance does not soften the old lines of a feud, it only reduces the number of people around who understand what is being settled, which leaves Jamil to account for himself to nobody in particular. Guilt, punishment and the possibility of stopping are the real subjects, and violence is filmed as a cost rather than a payoff.

Stevie tells her new town that she is a diplomat's daughter, and for a while the invention holds. She is fourteen. Her parents have moved the family to a small German province for reasons of their own, and they treat adulthood as a costume that can be taken off at will, so Pia Marais watches the daughter quietly put it on instead: the one working to look respectable, to have friends whose parents approve, to be ordinary on purpose. Ninety-five minutes, most of them inside a house filling steadily with her parents' friends and hangers-on. The stories of grandeur cost nothing to tell and a great deal to keep running. What the film wants is the exact price of being the only person in a household keeping accounts.

Somebody commissions an investigation into the problem of England without specifying what the problem is. Patrick Keiller answers with seventy-eight minutes of ports, power stations, prisons and manufacturing plants, narrated by a man who travels with a companion named Robinson whom the camera never shows. Seven excursions, 1997, a Tiger Award, and a documentary about a country conducted largely at its loading bays. The literary connections are real digressions, and so are the occasional stretches of ordinary landscape, which arrive like relief and are not permitted to last. England here is a working country rather than a pictured one. What holds it is the mismatch between the voice, precise and faintly amused, and the things it insists on looking at: fences, cranes, container stacks, the parts of an economy never composed to be seen.

A wealthy Bangkok house, a bed that cannot be left, and two men who would otherwise never have shared a room. The paralysed son belongs to money; the nurse hired to keep him comfortable comes from Isan, in the north of Thailand, and Anocha Suwichakornpong keeps both facts present in every exchange between them. Eighty-two minutes, and no hurry to push the friendship into shape. Care is intimate and care is also employment, and the intimacy does not cancel the wage. Neither man chose the other, and neither can leave the arrangement without cost. What accumulates is less a plot than a pressure: a body that must be handled, a class arrangement reproduced daily inside one bedroom, and two people who begin, cautiously, to talk to each other.

One day, ninety minutes, and a stretch of country where Slovakia runs into Moravia. Marek is eighteen and lives with his father among friends whose racism is the water he swims in; his dog is the only attachment in his life that asks nothing and answers plainly. Mira Fornay works in Slovak, on a border that functions less as a line than as a habit of thinking about who belongs on which side. The compression matters. Everything the film has to say about inheritance it must say inside a single day, with no montage and no year passing to soften the arithmetic. It carried the Golden Kingfisher Award for best feature and went forward as an international submission to the Academy Awards. Cruelty here is not dramatic. It is ordinary, and the ordinariness is what the film is watching.

The plan is to get Metallica into a room with Kabul Dreams, Afghanistan's first rock band. The man holding the plan is a writer whose sense of his own gifts exceeds anything the people around him are prepared to grant, and Babak Jalali plays that gap for a comedy that never tips over into farce: ninety minutes in Farsi in which the ambition and the available means stay stubbornly far apart. What keeps the film from being a joke at the writer's expense is that the ambition is not ridiculous. Putting an Afghan band in the same frame as Metallica is a serious idea about who is permitted into the room, and only the logistics, the interruptions and the ordinary business of a working day make it look absurd. Audiences at IFFR gave it their award.

Off-season in La Perrera there are nearly as many dogs as men. David has failed his university examinations and has a year to sit them again; his father, who considers the education a waste of time, offers terms instead of an argument: stay at the coastal house, study, and build himself somewhere to sleep. Manolo Nieto takes a hundred and eight minutes over that bargain, and the length is not indulgence. It is the only way to register how a resort town where nobody hurries and favours do the work of contracts gets into a city student's bones. The comedy is dry and mostly at the student's expense. What ends up under examination is not the syllabus but whether a year in that place leaves a man able to sit anything at all.

A doctor who has stopped practising is not the same thing as a man out of work. Axel is about forty, staying with his sister and her children, occupying rooms rather than living in them, and Santiago Loza is exact about the difference between idleness and suspension. Eighty-eight minutes, made in Argentina in 2003, pitched almost entirely below the level at which drama usually operates. Then a pregnant young woman appears and something like a couple forms, provisional and tender, held together mostly by the fact that neither of them has anywhere else to be. A pregnancy is a clock, and it is the only clock in the film. Loza never raises his voice about any of it. The risk he takes is asking attention for a life that has stopped asking anything of itself.

Between the father and the son there is no shared language and, by now, no need for one. The son does not hear or speak; the terms were settled years ago. Mohammad Shirvani builds eighty-five minutes out of episodes rather than a story, encounters that repeat with variations, each turning the same screw. The father is large, unwell and used to being obeyed, and the son is the instrument through which he gets what he wants. Whatever this father wants, the film is more interested in the arrangement that lets him have it. Then a woman arrives whose identity the film declines to fix, and the closed circuit acquires a term it cannot absorb. The genre labels attached to it, drama and fantasy and mystery, work less as description than as notice that no explanation is coming.
